comments.author: @UnknownFrequenciesWar
comments.text:
It's amazing how geography acts as a double-edged sword. Some countries found literal treasure hidden beneath hostile landscapes (like Australia's deserts or Norway's rocky coasts), while others had to literally engineer their survival and success (like Singapore expanding its land and the Netherlands fighting the sea).
Makes you wonder: in the upcoming AI and tech-driven era, will physical geography and natural resources continue to dictate wealth, or will human capital and digital infrastructure completely rewrite this list? What do you guys think?

replies.author: @ichneu
replies.text:
I believe that human capital and innovation will always remain important. AI, too, is built upon these foundations.
In this context, it is perhaps worth noting that the small nation of the Netherlands—roughly the size of Maryland—ranks third globally as an agricultural exporter, trailing only the USA and Brazil.
This is all the more remarkable when you consider that 539 people live here per square kilometer.

replies.author: @FortuneOfNations
replies.text: Singapore hints at one answer: it had no resources at all, and its fortune came from location plus a port, land and water it built itself. Then again, data centers crave cheap power and cool air, which could give Iceland and Norway a new edge. Will geography matter less, or just differently?
